speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS AND WELCOME TO NEW LEADER OE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already congratulated my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition on his accession to the leadership of his party, and I should like to congratulate him today on his election to the House of Commons and the taking of his seat in this chamber. In offering congratulations, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could call attention to the fact that he is succeeding in Colchester-Hants a member of quiet sincerity and friendly disposition who had won the affection of all members of this house who knew him.
It is interesting, at least it was interesting to me during the deep research I have conducted on this subject in the last few hours, to realize that the hon. Leader of the Opposition is the third member of his party who has held this post in the last 30 years who had previously served as premier of his province. I can assure the hon. gentleman of my design and my desire to co-operate with him in every possible way, as of course should be the case between two men who are endeavouring to serve the country in the two most important positions in the House of Commons.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I hasten to add, Mr. Speaker, that I do not include in that offer of co-operation the realization of the hon. gentleman's announced patriotic duty to bring about without delay a general election. I consider it my patriotic duty to save the country from a general election for as long as possible, though I do not expect any co-operation from the other side of that high endeavour.
The hon. gentleman assured Canadians the other night in a television broadcast that, among other things, he was anxious to make parliament work more effectively. I look forward to working with him in every way I can in the achievement of this important goal. There are other ways in which, subject to our different parliamentary and party responsibilities, I know we will be able to collaborate; but whether in collaboration or in criticism, in approval or in disapproval, I know the hon. gentleman who has now taken his seat is actuated, as I hope and believe we all are in this house, only by a desire and a resolve to serve Canada.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS AND WELCOME TO NEW LEADER OE OPPOSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS AND WELCOME TO NEW LEADER OE OPPOSITION
speechtext: In that spirit, Mr. Speaker, we on this side convey to him our best wishes as he takes on new and important responsibilities in this house.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS AND WELCOME TO NEW LEADER OE OPPOSITION
speechtext: In a more serious vein, I wish to extend on behalf of our group our heartiest congratulations to the Leader of the Opposition on his election as leader of his party, and to welcome him to the House of Commons. If I might add a personal note, I had the privilege of working with him at one or two federal-provincial conferences. I know him to be a man of high dedication, good judgment and sound common sense. As Leader of the Opposition he takes on a heavy responsibility. From his past record and from my brief association with him I am convinced that he will discharge his responsibilities in a manner which will bring credit to himself, distinction to his party and benefit to the people of Canada.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS AND WELCOME TO NEW LEADER OE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party would not miss the opportunity to add a few words of welcome to those addressed by the right hon. Prime Minister to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to whom we should like to say that we have followed attentively the evolution of his party, particularly the selection made the supporters of a democratic government in his riding.
We most sincerely congratulate the new Leader of the Opposition and wish him to work with all the parties in the house for the future of Canada, which means that we assume the opposition will work seriously

and constructively, not negatively. On the other hand, our party will always stand ready to co-operate with the other parties toward the objective of all Canadians, that is the progress of the country through ever more advanced, ever more sincere legislation for the economic development of the country.
I trust that the new Leader of the Opposition will bring to this parliament a constructive factor, and I am sure that if we all work hand in hand in the house, we shall succeed in an action not likely to destroy Canadian unity but to make it stronger still.

maintopic: CONGRATULATIONS AND WELCOME TO NEW LEADER OE OPPOSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as yesterday we joined in words of good wishes to the hon. member for Ontario, so today we join in welcoming the Leader of the Opposition as he takes his seat in the House of Commons. We as parliamentarians have a common responsibility and face a tremendous challenge. To the extent that we can work together in the interest of the nation and the solution of its problems, this responsibility rests on us all. If the Leader of the Opposition can use his influence to give direction, and if he can point the way for the leaders of his party to play a constructive role in this house, then to that extent we shall be in his debt. In this way we join in the expressions of welcome to him this afternoon.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pennell for the second reading of Bill No. C-168, to amend the Criminal Code.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill introduced by the hon. Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Pennell), on behalf of the government, is intended to abolish, for a period of five years, the death penalty for murderers, except in the case of murder of police officers, prison guards and other employees of the same category, acting in the course of their duties.
The said bill, if passed and put into force, could remain the law of the land if, within five years, the House of Commons and the Senate request it by resolution.
To my mind, the government is bringing down undesirable legislation, because the question has already been decided by the house last year and nothing, no major event, has happened since, likely to alter the situation. The valuable time of this parliament should rather be spent in finding quickly an efficient remedy to poverty, unemployment, inflation, to the most disquieting increase in the cost of living, and to increasing productivity.
As a matter of fact, in the spring of 1966, the House of Commons voted down 179 to 74, an amendment to a bill similar to the one now before us, also seeking the abolition of capital punishment except in cases of murder of policemen and prison guards.
Why does the government so soon renew the attempt after the house has taken a position so obvious and so decisive?
Is the present government mocking the democratic decision of the representatives of the Canadian people? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are discovering such an autocratic government.
On the very principle of retention or abolition of capital punishment, on April 5, 1966,
4312	COMMONS
Amendments Respecting Death Sentence the House of Commons made a definite decision, at least for the duration of this twenty-seventh parliament, for the retention of capital punishment by a vote of 143 to 112.
In spite of this clear majority decision, the government, within a few months and under the same parliament, submits anew the same subject matter of an amendment that was voted down by a solid majority of 105 votes.
Does the government consider hon. members of this house so fickle as to change their opinion from one season to another? I think the present government, Mr. Speaker, is wavering in irresponsibility and equivocation. Furthermore, the present government makes a mockery of existing legislation and of the views of the majority of the members elected by the Canadian people since they have commuted to life imprisonment all death sentences that were brought before them since April 1966. That is contempt of parliament, arrogance and faint-heartedness.
If the government wants all Canadians to respect the law as it stands today, let it set the example. That is the price we must pay to obtain better results in establishing public peace and order.
I am convinced that hon. members are consistent and that this bill will be defeated. If such a question must be brought up again for consideration, I feel that it should be dealt with by a future parliament. Then, the whole principle of abolition or retention of the death penalty, in every case, can be dealt with.
Everyone in this house knows that I favour retention of the death penalty. Indeed, on page 1748 and following of Hansard for May 30, 1958, as well as on page 3271 and following of Hansard for March 28, 1966, one can read the arguments I put forward and still uphold for the retention of the death penalty to serve as an efficient deterrent of capital murder, as an appropriate punishment, as a protection for the prison administration, as a means of eliminating as much as possible the increase in professional criminals, and as an example.
In my statement of March 28, 1966, I disclosed to the house the results of a survey I made in the riding of Sherbrooke, and the conclusions arrived at after consulting the members of the junior chamber of commerce of Sherbrooke. In the first case, 88 per cent of the replies favoured retention. In the second instance, 73 per cent of the members of the junior chamber of commerce of Sherbrooke opposed abolition of the death penalty.

DEBATES	November 15, 1967
I can tell the house that since March 28, 1966, the same views are being held and the great majority of my electors object, like I do, to any amendment to the Criminal Code on this important point.
Besides, the bill introduced by the Solicitor General proves unsatisfactory and contradictory in several respects. I shall point out a few of them.
The bill retains hanging merely with a view to protecting prison guards and police officers, as a deterrent of capital murder. It is a clear admission that capital punishment helps to restrain murderers. Now, if hanging is still a great deterrent of murders in the case of prison guards and police officers, it remains so just as much in the case of other citizens.
Those exceptions made for two groups of citizens, in the performance of their duties, imply a discriminatory attitude towards other human lives. As far as I know, we all have equal rights to live and to have our life protected.
Suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. Solicitor General, accompanied by a guard, should visit a penitentiary and that two prisoners would kill them both. In one case, the criminal would be hanged because he would have killed the guard, while the other would be spared because he would have killed the Solicitor General. Mr. Speaker, I have too much respect for the life of the hon. Solicitor General whom I consider as useful to society as that guard. That is why I cannot accept such an imbroglio. Furthermore, let us be more logical. Why should we give more protection to prison guards and police officers? These people are professionals; they are often armed and protected from murderers, while the great majority of citizens who are quietly attending to their business do not expect to be killed and would deserve as much protection, if not more.
Statistics show that, since 1945, in Canada, out of about 250 capital murders, only four guards in federal penitentiaries were murdered and only 19 police officers have suffered the same fate, that is hardly 9 per cent of victims.
What does the government do, through the medium of its bill, to prevent murderers from killing other citizens, representing 89 per cent of the victims since 1945, such as bank employees and the innocent victims of jealousy and revenge? What is the government doing also to protect judges, lawyers, court officials and private detectives?
November 15, 1967

It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is an incoherent text which does not even call into question again the basic principles of the matter under consideration.
I ask hon. members to do as I am doing, to kill this bill right now and to hold it up to ridicule.
It will have shown once more that the present government is a past master at wavering, equivocating and fumbling.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to insist on the obvious contradictions of some hon. members of the house, particularly the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who sits on the government side.
I read again, in the official report of the house, the position he took in 1966 on this important issue. I noted on page 1060, where he expressed very vigorously and with much conviction, on February 10, 1966, his first views on this important question of the maintenance or abolition of capital punishment. As shown on pages 1060 and 1061, he said:
-I respectfully submit that the prospective debate on capital punishment should be delayed as much as possible because I think the time is not ripe for such a debate, for the following reasons:
-among various reasons, he said that:
-from 1961 to 1965, there was, in the province of Quebec, an average of 57 murders per year, that is 28 per cent more during the period when the new government mitigated the penalty by commuting death sentences.
The stand taken by the hon. member for Lotbiniere is very clear. He said in the house that day that it was not the moment to deal with this question in view of the increase in the number of crimes committed between 1961 and 1965 which, incidentally, is still rising.
Moreover, on March 24, 1966, in his great speech on the main motion, the hon. member for Lotbiniere denied the federal cabinet the right to commute death sentences. He advanced many arguments in favour of the maintenance of capital punishment.
I wish to refer the hon. member for Lotbiniere and the other hon. members to the eloquent plea he addressed to the house on that occasion.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Now, how come the hon. member for Lotbiniere has changed his mind this year? Does he want to back up this government, who takes the members of this house for changelings, for reintroducing a specific

Amendments Respecting Death Sentence issue which was rejected last year by a significant majority, namely, 105 votes. Does this government expect the same members to change their mind, when called upon to vote on the same issue, the same principle?
Well, I did find one changeling in the house, namely, the hon. member for Lotbiniere. To this effect, I would refer you to the vote taken on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Montreal-Cartier (Mr. Klein). As a matter of fact, this amendment called for the withdrawal of the main motion, that is, to retain the death penalty only when the victims were jail guards or police officers.
We see on page 3910 of Hansard that the hon. member for Lotbiniere voted against that amendment. He now says that he will support a motion on the same subject matter brought forward by his government. This is a glaring contradiction, unworthy of hon. members of this house who, from one week to the other, want to change their minds about such basic and important matters.
I understand that, this year, the motion is brought forward by the government of which he is a member-there is probably some partisanship involved-while last year, it was moved by several members of the government and opposition who were asking for a free vote. But this year, the motion is brought forward by the government itself and we see the hon. member for Lotbiniere change his mind. This is unfortunately what we call partisanship when such an important issue is involved.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, with respect to this amendment of the hon. member for Cartier, we notice that nine ministers, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) have voted against the amendment that contains essentially the motion introduced by this government and the Prime Minister.
Well, let us be logical at least if we want the Canadian people to believe that their representatives are consequential and logical, specially on such important matters. And I notice in this vote taken on this amendment in 1966 which is substantially the same as the government motion, that nine ministers and the Prime Minister have voted against it, that is, to maintain total capital punishment, without any exception.
Well, how can the hon. Prime Minister and these nine ministers, after hardly a few months, vote quite logically and decently for a motion they defeated last year on an

We notice also that the hon. Registrar General (Mr. Turner) shows an attitude somewhat more logical than the hon. member for Lotbiniere, because last year, in 1966, the hon. Registrar General had voted for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cartier. He had voted for the retention of capital punishment only for the murderers of prison guards and policemen. This week, he has indicated that he would vote for the motion introduced by the government of which he is a supporter. Here at least is a logical man. The right hon. Prime Minister, through his cabinet, is going to vote for something which he condemned last year. This is known as tergiversation, a policy of procrastination on the part of the present government which has an effect not only on this most important moral and social question, but on all sectors of the Canadian economy.
I shall conclude here my brief remarks. I urge all the hon. members whose name appears in Hansard, who voted last year on the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Klein) and rejected it as being unacceptable, in accordance with their conscience and because they believed it necessary to retain capital punishment in Canada for the various reasons that were given, to behave in a way that is logical, and seemly and shows that they are aware of their responsibilities. Therefore, I invite the hon. members on the government side as well as on the opposition side, who voted against that amendment last year, to vote the same way, so that the Canadian people may realize that we, the legislators, are not weathercocks, people who say one thing today and who will say the opposite tomorrow. The Canadian people must be conscious of the fact that when their legislators rise to speak in this house, they do so with a sense of responsibility, after thoughtful, consideration and not on the spur of the moment, liable to change their mind the following week, and that when we vote on a question we do so knowledgeably, conscientiously and permanently.

An abolitionist does not become an abolitionist overnight. Let us be honest about this. Abolitionists have formed their views gradually over the years after searching their hearts and looking into this matter. Possibly they were retentionists before they did so. Last night the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Alken-brack), I believe it was, told the house that in the first two years of abolition in Great Britain the murder rate had risen. I am sorry the hon. member is not in the house at the present time but 1 should like to point out for the benefit of those who are in the house that right here in Canada in 1958 and 1959 33 people were murdered compared with 19 people in the two previous years, an increase of about 8 per cent. This only goes to illustrate that sound judgment on any matter cannot be made on the basis of short-term statistics. This is why the Solicitor General has asked that the abolition of the death penalty be given a five-year test period.
Like many other straight abolitionists I am not satisfied with the bill as it is. But I honestly feel it is a forward step. As an abolitionist I would like to have seen these reservations left out. Incidentally, most of us have been members of this house for a considerable period now and I think we would all agree that without doubt one of the finest pleas for abolition this parliament has ever heard was that made by the Solicitor General the other day. In the course of his speech he pointed out that the reservation affecting police officers and others in similar position would, if nothing else, give moral support to the men and women engaged in law enforcement, people who, by the way, are doing a terrific job for us in Canada.
Realizing there are many who wish to speak and that time is limited I should like to deal with three points before I sit down. First, can something be done for the convict and for society by imposing life imprisonment rather than capital punishment? It seems to me this is a most important consideration. I want my retentionist friends to search their souls. Is capital punishment fair to people in all walks of life?
I could go into many individual cases which might throw light on whether a person serving a life sentence can be of value to society. I will confine my examples to two prominent cases that everyone knows about. Consider the case of Robert Stroud, the celebrated bird man of Alcatraz who became a

There is a saying that the rich man may find it pretty difficult to enter the kingdom of heaven, but there are far fewer rich men who ever enter the execution chamber. I ask hon. members to think of the little man who elected them to represent him. Think about him when he comes before the courts without any money. I know of one case where the prosecution spent $40,000 and the little man, the defendant, had one lawyer and about $1,800 or $2,000 for his defence. That is justice in our courts. To my way of thinking this points out a very grave weakness in the administration of the justice in democratic countries. No matter how we may look at it, the little man with no money is left holding the bag, whether it is his neck that is at stake or whether he may be facing a period of time in jail.
Many years ago Thomas Jefferson said, "I shall ask for the abolition of the punishment of death until I have the infallibility of human judgment demonstrated to me." This brings me to my third point, that the possibility of a mistake is always present. Michigan Senator Philip A. Hart pointed out in a recent speech before the senate that error in court proceedings is not an extreme rarity. He went on to point out that during the period 1889 to 1927 of 406 persons sent to Sing Sing for execution 50 were found, upon reconsideration, to have been sentenced in error. Yet we are told that there is no chance of an error in our courts. Here is proof. It bears repeating, and I am going to repeat it, that out of 406 persons sent to Sing Sing for execution 50 were found, upon reconsideration, to have been sentenced in error. I know the retentionists will say, that the 50 got off but the very fact that such error could happen leaves one with a feeling that some of the remaining 356 might very easily have been innocent also.
None of us wants to face death, but to have the noose put around your neck or walk into the gas chamber must be an awful death. I think I can take as much as any man. I have gone through a lot in life, but I think this would be one of the hardest deaths Jack Roxburgh could face.

Curtain countries, have abolished the death penalty. Mississippi has not abolished it. I say to hon. members opposite who I person-naly know are retentionists, are you putting yourselves in the same class as the people of Mississippi who are a disgrace to the United States? Are you putting yourself in that class? If you vote for the retention of the death penalty in this country you will certainly be doing that. As of September 6, 1966 the answers are: (a) Quebec 9. (b) The dates presently set by the Courts for execution are: September 23, 1966 (1 person); September 30, 1966 (3 persons); October 14, 1966 (1 person); December 9, 1966 (1 person); December 16, 1966 (2 persons); January 13, 1967 (1 person);
Since that list was published, the matter of executions has never come up and the minister of justice of that time chose to hand in his resignation.
Amendments Respecting Death Sentence
This bill proposes something rather strange, that is to restrict capital punishment. It is a rather strange proposal in my opinion, since that punishment has been non existent for four years. How come, within the present legislation, gangsters who have murdered police officers, have never been put to death? The answer to that question perhaps lies with the R.C.M.P. as we learn from a report in 1'Action, a Quebec newspaper, of January 18, 1966, under the heading:
"Crime syndicates are developing rapidly in Canada for three reasons", which I take the liberty to quote:
According to R.C.M.P. report, crime syndicates in Canada related to the American mafia are developing rapidly because of political corruption, fear and inadequately applied laws.
The report goes on to say that to continue to prosper, organized bands of criminals must have two assets: inadequate application of laws resulting partly from the division of jurisdiction between the federal, provincial and municipal governments, and protection against trials and interventions.
"To secure such an immunity, they have to pay bribes to persons having a certain authority in the police, municipal administrations and to politicians."
Mr. Speaker, I think that this article is self-explanatory, and I still say that this bill will deprive the people of their rights. It might be true that police officers are in danger and that their life is at stake sometimes, but that is debatable if one considers that other people are in danger, such as clerks in stores and watchmen in some buildings. Those people are all the more in danger because they lack the training and the weapons of the police officers to protect themselves.
I submit that the proposal to retain the death penalty only for the murderers of police and law officers and prison guards is a strange one and that, if unfortunately it were adopted, it would give dubious results.
Several factors make it impossible to appraise a human being. It is unfortunate that in order to manage to save a few heads, the government had to decide in favour of classifying the victims. Why put more emphasis on punishing the murderer of a bachelor police officer and consider the killing of a head of family as a second degree murder? How can one ignore the murder of an irreplaceable mother and think only of protecting a prison guard who can be replaced at any time on the mere recommendation of a political organizer?
If the bill under consideration were to be passed, what treatment would be meted out to those who take pleasure in planting bombs

Imagine a revolution during which hundreds of persons would be killed. On the basis of the present bill, it is clear that the murderers would simply be imprisoned, but it would merely take the arrival of a Castro to open all the prisons and all those murderers would be decorated and treated as heroes. The murder, as provided in this bill, would be a capital murder inasmuch as the corpse would meet the requirements of the classifiers.
As the manager of a business during many years, I have sent to the slaughter-house several heads of cattle. There is a scale of grades in such a business. If you send a steer to the slaughter-house, for example, it will be graded choice No. 1 or choice No. 2. There is the first grade, medium grade and commercial grade. In the case of fresh pork, it will be graded A, B or C and downgraded if it is too fatty. However, in the case of human beings, the law simplifies this classification, in the sense that the ordinary citizen is excluded, and only those who wear a policeman's badge, a tin star, as they say, before the massacre, are being considered.
The list of people for whom this bill provides protection is too short, I think, and this makes it unacceDtable. I know that several members are of the same opinion.
On looking over Hansard of Friday, November 10, on page 4163, we find that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Cho-quette) suggested a longer list. Since he has no family, this member, in his eloquent appeal for additional protection, has thought of his spiritual leader, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson). He also suggested another name, that is, our national father, the governor general.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH SENTENCE AND LIFE IMPRISONMENT
speechtext:
I shall vote against this bill because I also know the views of the voters in my constituency. During the winter of 1966, I held a sort of referendum in my riding on the retention of capital punishment. Out of 3,125 replies received at that time in answer to my questionnaire, 2,978 supported the retention of capital punishment whereas 147 were against it. I am preciously keeping all these letters which bear the signature and address of every citizen who has made it his duty to express an opinion.
Now, the percentage of those who favour retaining capital punishment is possibly higher in Portneuf than in other ridings of the country and I think there are three reasons for that.
First, there is envy. The workers, the taxpayers in the constituency of Portneuf are envious of the royal treatment given to bandits in penitentiaries, because where former inmates come back to see us, they explain how they are fed and we realize that 60 per cent of the population of the country cannot afford such food and such menus.
The citizens of Portneuf are envious also of the long holidays of various duration given to certain bandits on the Florida or California coasts.
The second reason, Mr. Speaker, is that the people of Portneuf have a long memory and here, the motto of Quebec "Je me souviens" takes another meaning. The citizens of Portneuf remember that in the Quebec area several young boys were strangled by a former inmate who had been sentenced to life imprisonment but who was liberated through certain influences. The people of my area also remember that the same prisoner escaped from jail in Quebec city, carrying the governor of the jail on his back.
These citizens also realize, Mr. Speaker, that the endless succession of trials held for those people, those individuals, those bandits, those murderers who normally should have been hanged a long time ago, is very costly for them.
The third reason, Mr. Speaker, is that Portneuf is situated on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, behind the constituency of Lotbiniere. Now, being situated behind the constituency of Lotbiniere does not prevent
November 15, 1967

Portneuf from being the most beautiful riding in the country and one of the most picturesque areas of the globe since we have the river, plains and mountains.
But, precisely, because it is situated behind the constituency of Lotbiniere, each time the citizens of Portneuf look to the other shore of the St. Lawrence they see the forests of Lotbiniere which were once changed into burial grounds. Every time we go to the south shore, when travelling to the Beauce or the Eastern Townships, we sometimes go to Sherbrooke because it is also a beautiful spot. It is also absolutely necessary to cross the riding of Lotbiniere. Well, every time we travel on those roads, we cannot help but think that we are driving on corpses. No mistake is possible: several miles of roads in the riding of Lotbiniere have already been paved with corpses.
All these events, Mr. Speaker, have contributed to enlighten my constituents who are extremely dissatisfied with the attitude of the present government in the last five years as regards the death penalty.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, for three days, some members have been plucking at our heartstrings by harping on the cruelty of it all. Well, I say to them that if it is cruel to execute a murderer, why not close all the prisons? Indeed, I feel that it is just as cruel to lock somebody up for the rest of his life. And what about this bill in regard to the financial crisis of the government?
Interesting figures are indeed given in this regard on page 2760 of the official report of March 16, 1966. It is expensive to keep a criminal in prison. I should like to quote some figures. As hon. members know, family allowances have remained the same for the last twenty years, but the cost of keeping a prisoner has increased in proportion to the rising cost of living.
In 1962-63, for instance, as is shown on page 2760 of the French version of the official report of March 16, 1966, it cost $2,572.65 to keep a single prisoner in minimum security institutions; in 1964-65, it cost $3,019.92.
Mr. Speaker, that means that one single prisoner costs more per day to the government than the monthly family allowances. Indeed, considering the fact that in our ridings widows and needy mothers, under our present welfare system, must be content with an allowance of $5.50 per day for a family of six, while the amount spent in our penal

institutions is $8.00 per day for each prisoner, it is obvious that the country cannot afford to finance a collection of bandits.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), that the debate be adjourned immediately.

PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OP SUMMER TRAINING COURSE OF CANADIAN YOUTH AS CENTENNIAL PROJECT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of including in its Centennial projects the formation of a training service for Canadian youths aged between 15 and 20 years under the responsibility of the Canadian Forces; this service to be on a voluntary basis and allow the youths to spend two or three months a year in various camps or military institutions throughout the country, alternating their stay from one year to the next in different regions of Canada; the whole project to be organized in co-operation with the Departments of Education of the various provinces and enable the teachers to join the Canadian Forces for the same period so that they might take an active part in this program; and such service to be one factor in uniting young Canadians who, through it, would learn to know each other better and to know their country, and develop a better spirit of discipline and citizenship, all within the framework of a program of physical and linguistic education.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the few minutes that will follow, we will have a debate which, in my opinion, may be somewhat more constructive than the one we have had for the last few days, at least it will be a debate that will make us look forward, since it concerns the Canadian youth.
Mr. Speaker, on two previous occasions, 1 introduced in the house a motion with a view of creating a compulsory training service for Canadian youths aged between 18 and 21 years of age.
Some members of this house may wonder why this year I have changed my project to make it voluntary and applicable only during the school holidays period.
For a very simple reason, Mr. Speaker. I realize more and more the advantages such a service of military training would have for our youth. I have also realized, however, that because of many sociological, political and economic factors, such a service, were it to be compulsory, could not be expected to be established within a short period of time.
I have therefore arrived at a compromise and I hope that all members of this house will support my proposal today, since it is urgent to provide our young people with a complementary educational and training sys-

Centennial Youth Summer Program tern which will, in my opinion, meet a growing need.
Our young people themselves suffer and, without realizing it, blame society which fails to provide them with all the means they need to develop in the twentieth century.
As a matter of fact, the development of our educational system and the great need of skills in this spatial and electronic era result in the production of specialists, but more and more formal education and the moulding of the character of the individual are overlooked.
Of course, I know, and Your Honour also, that the government is seeking now much more to find means of reducing its expenses than to introduce legislation aiming at increasing the taxpayers' burden.
Nevertheless, the fact remains that priorities must be exercised, and I for one believe that tomorrow's generation should have priority nowadays.
Obviously, there is no question of asking the government, at the present time to spend millions of dollars at once, but to suggest that an exhaustive study be undertaken, whether directly by the staff of the department or through referral of the matter to the national defence committee, with respect to the advantages of such a project and on its social and economic implications.
Mr. Speaker, very few will deny the benefits of a stay of a few months or of a few years in a military institution or in our armed forces. Many hon. members have known military life personally and now acknowledge that they derived significant benefits from it.
Most of us know our cadet corps, our militia units, our active units, our military colleges, etc., which are all permament testimonials to what military training brings to young people and to the fact that it gives them the opportunity to support one another in an environment where authority is recognized by everyone and, especially, appreciated because it is respected and undisputed.
In this motion, Mr. Speaker, I only propose, in fact, the establishment of a civic training program, which is more than is now offered through cadet corps, and that could be done through a reorientation of the present program of cadet corps with the possibility of increasing their number considerably during the holidays while extending a little the training period during that time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes available I can only say in general terms that I congratulate the hon. member for directing the attention of the house to an important, timely and perhaps timeless matter. It is not only in our own time that the youthful generation is disquieted about those of us who are of riper years, as the prayer book puts it. It is not only now that the young have called their elders "squares'1, or whatever the modern jargon of the day happened to be.
Having made that general and sound sociological observation, I think we do live in an age when there is an excessive restlessness among our youth which we disregard at our peril. It behooves all public people at all levels of government to note carefully the way in which their institutions take note of what is sometimes called the generational revolt.
We live in an age of restlessness and protest; we live in an age when people, both young and old, are more mobile than ever before. I am attracted by the suggestion that we should find some means whereby groups of young people might move from one part of the country to another. I am attracted by the idea that in the process of living together there could be a greater facility and felicity developed in the two languages of this country. This development is something to be desired. Some of us in our mid-forties may not become proficient bilingually before we reach our mid-fifties, although we might try, but I think the people in younger groups might succeed and any attempt in this regard would be a notable, and perhaps noble, service on the part of the government.
I cannot comment on the details of the hon. member's program. I am not a military expert and I do not know what would be the demands of such a program upon the existing institutions. Nor do I know the problems which might be presented to the military establishment in training of a group which would be at best, quasi-militaristic. This problem would require a good deal more consideration.
November 15, 1967

Centennial Youth Summer Program
The suggestion that emphasis be placed upon training in language and in physical education is one that I heartily commend. Being neither an outstanding physical specimen of manhood nor an outstanding linguist I can say that had a program like this been in effect 20 or 30 years ago things might have been better from a personal standpoint. In a more serious vein, I believe this is the kind of thing we should be thinking of more often in this legislative chamber, particularly when very often we seem bound to become a mill for grinding out a lot of legislation, some of which is pretty tedious and much of which is controversial. We should take a look at some of those things which are more fundamental to the over-all life process and look at some of the values of this society we seek to serve rather than concentrate merely on the mechanics of existing institutions of that society. To this extent I should like to commend the hon. member for bringing our attention to this matter of importance.
I have seen a few proposals like this in recent years and I think this is altogether wholesome and good. If this can be done through the existing Department of National Defence, with co-operation from the departments of education, it is a splendid idea. If it does no more than bring about a greater degree of co-operation among provincial departments of education this would be a very favourable step. We suffer greatly from too much differentiation from province to province in the field of education. There are far too many tight little empires built in departments of education all across the land, and I believe our young people are suffering as a consequence. In a highly mobile society such as ours this should be looked at in a corrective way. Therefore I should like to commend the hon. member for his thoughtful contribution on a very important matter.

Mr. Speaker, under normal circumstances, I would have been most happy today to join with my colleague for Beauhamois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel), not only to support, but also to promote his very interesting motion.
Unfortunately, we all know what sad fate is in store for motions of this type under the obsolete rules of the house. In spite of my personal feelings expressed on other occasions with regard to the practice of killing

bills, to my regret, I must use up the last remaining minutes to congratulate my colleague for Beauharnois-Salaberry and ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ca-dieux)-who, I noticed, has listened very carefully to my colleague's suggestions, even though we will not have much success today -to see to it that his department which is under such a competent and able management-and I congratulate the minister on his recent appointment-take it upon itself to introduce a bill which would then be much more acceptable.
Far from me, Mr. Speaker, the thought of creating a tide of marked militarism, something about which many of our compatriots are always suspicious and rightly so. I have taken due note of the principle laid down in the motion, that service would be on a voluntary basis. Having had the opportunity of witnessing the efficiency of summer holiday training of cadets, for instance at the Farn-harm camp in the eastern townships, I can only agree that our youth is greatly lacking in the spirit of discipline, of order and ef respect for the established authority, at every level.
They no longer believe in anything, or anybody, follow any instructions, wherever they come from. The spirit of unconditional freedom, if I may use the expression, cannot fail to cause us deep concern. I think that this is one of the best ways to counter this mad race to the sorry rules of anarchy and revolution.
Mr. Speaker, the house is aware of the unfortunate happenings nowadays, in sorry associations or communities of hippies, beatniks and others, who feed on LSD, marijuana or free love, and it is with measures like the one proposed by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry that we undoubtedly will fight more efficiently and get better results.
Mr. Speaker, in closing and in view of the fact that we can make no further progress today, I express the wish once again that this idea will not become a dead letter in the pigeon holes that are already bulging with forgotten files of the House of Commons. I am convinced that the hon. Minister of National Defence, who understands the problem well, will consult his senior officers and implement in a tangible way with more chances of success if the initiative is taken

by the government, the bill advocated by my colleague, which I support with all the sincerity I am capable of.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is now six o'clock. I look forward to the government's action.
